newsitem.title: USA: Dollar surges against mark after Lebed ousted.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surges against mark after Lebed ousted.

text.p: The dollar surged against the German mark Thursday after Russian President Boris Yeltsin, in a surprise move, dismissed security chief Alexander Lebed for alleged insubordination.

The mark typically suffers from political instability in Russia given Germany's geographical proximity and economic links with the country. The dollar also is seen as a safe haven during political unrest, as is the Swiss franc.

The charismatic Lebed, who had only held office for four months, was dismissed in a speech on national television by Yeltsin, who cited Lebed's lack of team spirit and obvious ambition to become Russia's next leader.
The dollar immediately jumped to 1.5454 marks, its highest level since May, on the news. It later settled a bit to close at 1.5427, up from 1.5400 in late trade Wednesday.
"The knee-jerk reaction was people see more instability in Russia so they sold the mark," said David Solin, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"But the big question is what happens to Lebed going forward. Apparently he is popular with voters and the lower ranks of the army," he said.
Lebed, an outspoken former paratrooper general, won a strong 15 percent of vote in the first round of Russia's presidential election last June.
The dollar's gains were limited by some investors' confidence the mark would not fall lower still and the hope that Lebed's dismissal will help stabilise Russian politics.
"It somewhat improves the short-term stability in Russia because it strengthens the hand of the Prime Minister and the people immediately around him," said Anne Mills, currency analyst at Lehman.
The Swiss franc gained versus the mark to 0.8225 from 0.8232 late Wednesday. The mark also gave back early gains against the Italian lira and French franc.
The dollar fell slightly against the Japanese yen to 112.19 yen from 112.30 yen late on Wednesday despite strong buying interest from Japan, dealers said.
Japanese importers, who must sell yen for dollars to pay for goods bought abroad, propped up the dollar with large buy orders, dealers said.
Trading slowed in the afternoon as dealers focused their attention on Friday's August trade report, which could jostle the dollar against the yen, dealers said.
The trade deficit in July ballooned to a record $11.68 billion, but analysts were expecting a smaller gap of $8.5 billion in August.
"I'm looking for a bit of movement tomorrow as the trade numbers come out," said Robert Fullem, trader at Nat West Markets in New York, referring to dollar-yen exchange rates.
The British pound rose to $1.5873 from $1.5842 late on Wednesday.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3521 from C$1.3548.
